Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.

slides.say: The rectangle in the accompanying figure is made of forty congruent squares, each with a side of one centimeter. What is the shaded area?
at: The rectangle in the accompanying figure

slides.say: What is the shaded shape? A trapezoid? Let's count its sides. One, two, three, four, five. It's a pentagon, and we never learned an area formula for it. We call these shaded-area questions, and there are two main approaches.

[short pause] One approach takes an area we know, the rectangle, and subtracts the white parts. The other breaks the shaded area into shapes we know, with completions or with symmetry. We'll see all of them. Subtracting is the main one, and the most common, so we start with it, the math way.
at: One approach takes an area we know

slides.say: The rectangle is eight by five, so its area is eight times five, forty. The white parts are four right triangles in the corners, and the area of a right triangle is leg times leg, over two.
at: so its area is eight times five

slides.say: Top left, the legs are three and two. Three times two is six, and over two that's three.
Top right, the legs are five and two. Five times two is ten, and over two that's five.
The two bottom ones have legs of two and three. Two times three is six, and half of six is three. So each one is three.

All the white parts together are three plus five plus three plus three, fourteen. Forty minus fourteen is twenty-six. Choice number three is our answer. Careful, fourteen, choice number one, is the white part, not the shaded part.
at: Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's use understanding: pair the pieces that make a whole. Many students count whole squares, and when two pieces of squares complete each other into one whole square, they count them as one.

Here the sloping sides cut squares into odd pieces, so we look at them in groups. Cut the grid into five rectangles, four in the corners and one in the middle. On top, three by two and five by two. At the bottom, two by three, four by three, and two by three.
at: Cut the grid into five rectangles

slides.say: Look at the top left rectangle, three by two. The sloping side goes from corner to corner, so every shaded piece has a white piece just like it, turned around. They complete each other, so the shaded part is half of six, three.
at: Look at the top left rectangle
so the shaded part is half of six

slides.say: The same in the other corners. Top right, half of ten is five. At the bottom, half of six is three, twice.
at: At the bottom, half of six
At the bottom, half of six

slides.say: The middle rectangle is all shaded. Four times three is twelve whole squares.
Three plus five plus three plus three plus twelve is twenty-six. Choice number three again.
[pause] And the third way, by understanding again, with the symmetry principle we already know. We break the shape into pieces we know. Draw a line between the two side corners of the pentagon.
Above the line there's a triangle. Its base is the whole width, eight, and its tip is on the top side of an eight by two rectangle. So it's half of sixteen, eight.
Below the line, the middle rectangle is four by three, twelve. And each side triangle is half of a two by three rectangle, half of six, three.

Eight plus twelve plus three plus three is twenty-six. Choice number three again. So in a shaded-area question, subtract the white parts from a shape you know, or break the shaded part into shapes you know. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
